summary: Defines an information model for describing the QoS mechanisms inside network devices, including hosts. It describes the properties common to selecting and conditioning traffic through a device's forwarding path, across both the differentiated services and integrated services architectures. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Routers have different traffic-sorting machines inside. This is a common vocabulary for describing those machines, so different makers' gear can be described in the same way.

questions: how to describe router qos mechanisms
what is the qos datapath information model
what is a conditioning service in qos
how does a token bucket meter work in diffserv
subtitle: A common vocabulary of classes for describing the traffic-handling machinery inside routers, switches and hosts.

tldr.problem: Devices from different makers condition traffic in different ways, so QoS policies could not be written once and applied to all of them without a shared description of the mechanisms inside.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3670 defines an information model of classes for classifiers, meters, markers, droppers, queues and schedulers, plus services and associations that chain them together along a device's forwarding path.
tldr.outcome: Together with the QoS Policy Information Model (RFC 3644), it lets policy rules configure and manage QoS mechanisms in a device-independent way. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 3670 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2004, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It is meant to be used with RFC 3644.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 3670 defines an information model for the quality of service (QoS) mechanisms inside network devices, including hosts. It covers the properties common to selecting and conditioning traffic through a device's forwarding path (the datapath), across both Differentiated Services (DiffServ) and Integrated Services (IntServ). Admission control for IntServ is not in scope.

The model is meant to be used with the QoS Policy Information Model (RFC 3644, called QPIM). This document describes the mechanisms, and QPIM describes policy rules that control them. An information model is independent of any particular repository, so it cannot be implemented directly. The RFC suggests vendors map the classes, directly or through a format like a COP-PR PIB, onto their own implementations.

The hierarchies are influenced by the DMTF's CIM Network QoS submodel and are deliberately not derived from the Policy Core Information Model (RFC 3060). Packet filtering reuses the FilterEntryBase and FilterList classes from RFC 3460.
sections.eli5: It is a shared list of names for the parts inside a router that sort, measure, mark and line up traffic, so people can talk about any router the same way.

sections.title: Why Model Mechanisms Separately from Policy
sections.content:
The RFC describes a policy continuum: high-level business policies, then device-independent policies, then device-dependent policies. This model supplies the device-independent layer, a common set of abstractions that different devices and vendors can share. The example in the text is a high-level rule, if protocol = HTTP, then mark with DSCP 24, which becomes configuration actions: create an HTTP filter, create a DSCP marker with the value 24, and bind the filter to the marker.

The RFC argues that QoS is a set of services that policy controls, not part of the policy itself. Two devices may both have a queue, but one may be a simple FIFO and another a more elaborate scheme. Policy controls these mechanisms rather than representing them, so the device model belongs in a device schema.

On attributes, the RFC rejects multiple synchronized properties and multi-modal properties, and chooses absolute values, leaving policy operators to handle percentages by multiplying.
sections.eli5: A boss says what should happen. A separate list says what tools each machine has. Keeping the two lists apart lets one boss instruct many different machines.

sections.title: QoS Services and Conditioning Services
sections.content:
The model is built around two class hierarchies tied together by associations. QoSService represents a higher-level service, such as a premium service, and has subclasses FlowService (flow-oriented) and DiffServService (aggregate-oriented, with an AFService subclass). Services can be nested with the QoSSubService aggregation, so a Gold Service can be built from two DiffServ services.

ConditioningService is the base class for the building blocks: classifiers, meters, markers, droppers, queues and schedulers. The model sets no fixed order. Instead, instances are chained with the NextService, NextServiceAfterMeter and NextServiceAfterClassifierElement associations, and ingress or egress interfaces are tied to their first or last service by dedicated associations. The routing decision in the device core is not modeled.

The model also departs from the DiffServ informal model by allowing information about ingress treatment to travel with a packet to egress. It does so through a PreambleMarkerService that appends <type>,<value> items such as ConformingFromMeter or VlanId, and a PreambleFilter that matches them.
sections.eli5: Think of an assembly line. A big job, like premium delivery, is made of small steps. Each step sorts, checks, labels, trims or queues packages, and arrows say which step comes next.

sections.title: Classifiers, Meters, Markers and Droppers
sections.content:
A classifier splits one traffic stream into several. Each ClassifierElement uses a FilterList, even if it holds one entry, and the entries in a list are ANDed together. A multi-field filter such as IPHeaderFilter can cover the IP 5-tuple and the DSCP in one object.

A MeterService checks packets against a traffic profile. Its MeterType values are 1 Other, 2 Average Rate, 3 Exponentially Weighted Moving Average, and 4 Token Bucket. The token bucket meter has AverageRate, PeakRate, BurstSize and ExcessBurstSize, and with an excess burst size it has three levels: conforming, partially conforming and non-conforming.

Markers write a value into a packet field. DSCPMarkerService writes a DSCPValue in the range 0..63 and leaves the other two bits of the DS field unchanged. There are also ToS, 802.1Q and preamble markers.

Droppers are either absolute, dropping everything in their queue, or algorithmic. A head or tail dropper compares queue lengths with a QueueThreshold, and a RED dropper uses smoothed queue inputs with minimum and maximum thresholds. A dropper drops from exactly one queue, tied by NextService, though it can look at several.
sections.eli5: A sorter puts packages into piles, a checker sees who is going too fast, a labeler stamps a mark on each one, and a trimmer throws packages away when the line gets too long.

sections.title: Queues and Schedulers
sections.content:
A QueuingService holds packets and a PacketSchedulingService decides when a queued packet is sent to an output interface. Its SchedulerType values are 1 Other, 2 FIFO, 3 Priority, 4 Allocation, 5 Bounded Priority and 6 Weighted Round Robin Packet.

Scheduling parameters are carried by SchedulingElement subclasses (allocation, weighted round robin, priority and bounded priority), bound to queues or to other schedulers, and schedulers are chained with NextScheduler. The RFC tests the design against four cases: a simple hierarchical scheduler, a complex one that needs two parameter sets per queue, an excess capacity scheduler built from a non-work-conserving scheduler, and a hierarchical class-based queuing (CBQ) scheduler, where the top scheduler holds 100% of link capacity and parcels it out in tiers.
sections.eli5: Queues are lines of packets waiting. A scheduler is the traffic cop who decides which line goes next, and cops can be stacked so a big cop gives each smaller cop a share of the time.

sections.title: The Class Hierarchy and Naming
sections.content:
Section 4 defines the classes, associations and aggregations. Many derive from CIM core classes such as Service. Associations and aggregations are classes of their own, they form a separate inheritance hierarchy, and all of those in this model are binary. Examples of the associations and aggregations defined are NextService and EntriesInFilterList.

The model mostly describes configuration. State is covered in a very limited way, only CurrentQueueDepth on QueuingService. An appendix explains how to name instances in a native CIM implementation.
sections.eli5: The class list is like a family tree of parts, from a general Service at the top down to specific kinds such as a token bucket meter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Like the policy core models, this document defines an information model that cannot be implemented directly. The RFC says security issues do not arise until the model is mapped to an implementable data model such as a MIB, PIB or LDAP schema. It refers readers to the policy core model for a general discussion and to the DiffServ MIB (RFC 3289) for the security implications of specific objects.
sections.eli5: This is only a blueprint, not a working machine, so the real safety questions come up when someone builds a real system from it.
